hcv_title: Bohr's Model and Physics of the Atom
notes: 11 Objective I items rebuilt. One source item asks students to pick a velocity-vs-n graph; re-cast as a question about how orbital speed scales with n. The 'which one-electron system is it?' items exercise the $ Z^{2} $ and $ 1/Z $ scalings and are kept as a pair.

practice_bank.title: Practice — Bohr's Model and the Atom
practice_bank.intro: Eleven questions on the hydrogen atom. Almost everything follows from three scalings: $ r \propto n^{2}/Z $, $ E \propto -Z^{2}/n^{2} $ and $ v \propto Z/n $.

sections.title: Quantisation and Orbits
sections.blurb: Angular momentum in units of h/2π.

items.prompt: The minimum orbital angular momentum of the electron in a hydrogen atom is
items.explanation: Bohr's condition is $ L = nh/2\pi $, and the smallest allowed $ n $ is 1, giving $ L = h/2\pi = \hbar $. This quantum of angular momentum is why $ \hbar $ appears throughout atomic physics — it is the natural unit in which nature measures spin and orbital motion.

items.prompt: As one considers orbits of higher $ n $ in a hydrogen atom, the electron's orbital **speed**
items.explanation: The three Bohr scalings are $ r \propto n^{2} $, $ v \propto 1/n $ and $ E \propto -1/n^{2} $. Outer electrons orbit larger circles more slowly — and since the period goes as $ r/v \propto n^{3} $, they take dramatically longer per orbit.

items.prompt: As $ n $ increases, the electric **potential energy** of a hydrogen atom
items.explanation: The potential energy is $ U = -2 \times 13.6/n^{2} $ eV — negative, and rising towards zero as $ n $ grows. Moving the electron further out means less tightly bound, hence *higher* (less negative) potential energy. Confusing 'larger magnitude' with 'larger value' is the trap here.

items.prompt: An atom or ion has a ground-state energy of $ -54.4 $ eV. It may be
items.explanation: For a one-electron system $ E_1 = -13.6\,Z^{2} $ eV. Setting this to $ -54.4 $ gives $ Z^{2} = 4 $, so $ Z = 2 $ — singly ionised helium. $ \text{Li}^{++} $ with $ Z = 3 $ would give $ -122.4 $ eV, and hydrogen or deuterium $ -13.6 $ eV.

items.prompt: The radius of the smallest orbit in a one-electron system is $ 18 $ pm. The system is
items.explanation: The Bohr radius scales as $ r_1 = 53/Z $ pm, so $ 18 $ pm gives $ Z = 53/18 \approx 3 $ — doubly ionised lithium. Note that radius goes as $ 1/Z $ while energy goes as $ Z^{2} $: a higher nuclear charge pulls the electron in *and* binds it much more tightly.

sections.title: Transitions and Spectral Lines
sections.blurb: One photon per jump, and what a set of photons reveals.

items.prompt: Three photons from an excited hydrogen sample have energies $ 12.1 $ eV, $ 10.2 $ eV and $ 1.9 $ eV. They must come from
options: a single atom, cascading all the way down
exactly two atoms, and no more
either two atoms or three atoms
exactly three atoms, and no fewer
items.explanation: Note that $ 10.2 + 1.9 = 12.1 $, so these are the $ 3\to1 $, $ 2\to1 $ and $ 3\to2 $ transitions. One atom falling $ 3\to2\to1 $ produces the $ 1.9 $ and $ 10.2 $ eV photons; another falling $ 3\to1 $ directly gives $ 12.1 $ eV. So two atoms suffice — but three atoms each making one transition also works.

items.prompt: Which transition in hydrogen emits the **longest** wavelength?
items.explanation: Longest wavelength means smallest energy gap. Levels crowd together as $ n $ rises, so $ 4 \to 3 $ has the smallest gap ($ 0.66 $ eV) of these, against $ 10.2 $ eV for $ 2 \to 1 $. Transitions to $ n = 1 $ are always the most energetic, which is why the Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet.

items.prompt: The ionisation energy of hydrogen from its ground state is
items.explanation: The ground state sits at $ -13.6 $ eV, so raising the electron to $ E = 0 $ — free, with no kinetic energy — costs exactly $ 13.6 $ eV. Note that $ 10.2 $ eV is the first *excitation* energy ($ n=1 \to 2 $), a quite different quantity.

items.prompt: A hydrogen atom in the $ n = 4 $ state can emit at most how many different wavelengths as it returns to the ground state?
items.explanation: The number of distinct transitions from level $ n $ down to the ground state is $ \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6 $ — namely $ 4\to3 $, $ 4\to2 $, $ 4\to1 $, $ 3\to2 $, $ 3\to1 $ and $ 2\to1 $. A single atom emits only one cascade, but a *sample* shows all six lines.

sections.title: What the Model Gets Right and Wrong
sections.blurb: Spectacularly successful for hydrogen, and only for hydrogen.

items.prompt: Bohr's model fails to account for
options: the spectrum of multi-electron atoms and the fine structure of lines
the existence of discrete energy levels
items.explanation: The model handles one-electron systems beautifully but cannot cope with electron-electron interactions, so it fails for helium onwards. It also offers no account of spectral fine structure, line intensities, or why the quantisation condition should hold — all of which needed quantum mechanics.

items.prompt: In Bohr's model, the electron's kinetic energy compared with the magnitude of its total energy is
items.explanation: For an inverse-square attraction, $ KE = -E $ and $ U = 2E $ — so the kinetic energy equals the magnitude of the total energy. In hydrogen's ground state that means $ KE = 13.6 $ eV and $ U = -27.2 $ eV. This is the virial theorem, and the same 2:1 relation governs satellite orbits.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — Radius and energy of Bohr orbits
worked_examples.problem: Find the radius and energy of the $ n = 3 $ orbit in hydrogen, and in $ \text{Li}^{++} $.
worked_examples.solution:
**The two scalings:** $ r_n = \frac{n^{2}}{Z}(53\ \text{pm}) $ and $ E_n = -\frac{13.6Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV} $

**Hydrogen ($ Z = 1 $), $ n = 3 $:**

$ r = 9(53) = 477\ \text{pm} $

$ E = -\frac{13.6}{9} = -1.51\ \text{eV} $

**$ \text{Li}^{++} $ ($ Z = 3 $), $ n = 3 $:**

$ r = \frac{9}{3}(53) = 159\ \text{pm} $

$ E = -\frac{13.6(9)}{9} = -13.6\ \text{eV} $

**Note the opposite dependences on $ Z $.** The radius shrinks as $ 1/Z $ while the binding energy grows as $ Z^{2} $ — a higher nuclear charge pulls the electron closer *and* holds it far more tightly. Nine times the binding energy at one third the radius.

**A coincidence worth noticing.** $ \text{Li}^{++} $ at $ n = 3 $ has exactly hydrogen's ground-state energy, because $ Z^{2}/n^{2} = 9/9 = 1 $. Any one-electron system with $ n = Z $ shares that energy.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Wavelength of a spectral line
worked_examples.problem: Find the wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen atom falls from $ n = 3 $ to $ n = 2 $ (the H-alpha line).
worked_examples.solution:
**Energy of each level:**

$ E_3 = -\frac{13.6}{9} = -1.51\ \text{eV} $

$ E_2 = -\frac{13.6}{4} = -3.40\ \text{eV} $

**Photon energy:**

$ \Delta E = E_3 - E_2 = -1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89\ \text{eV} $

**Wavelength**, using $ \lambda(\text{nm}) = 1240/E(\text{eV}) $:

$ \lambda = \frac{1240}{1.89} = 656\ \text{nm} $

**This is the red H-alpha line** — the brightest line in the Balmer series, and the reason hydrogen-rich nebulae photograph red.

**Watch the sign convention.** Both energies are negative, and the *difference* must come out positive since a photon is emitted. Subtracting the wrong way round gives a negative photon energy, which should stop you immediately.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Series limits
worked_examples.problem: Find the shortest and longest wavelengths of the Lyman series in hydrogen.
worked_examples.solution:
The Lyman series consists of all transitions ending at $ n = 1 $.

**Shortest wavelength (series limit)** — from $ n = \infty $:

$ \Delta E = 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6\ \text{eV} $

$ \lambda = \frac{1240}{13.6} = 91.2\ \text{nm} $

**Longest wavelength** — from the nearest level, $ n = 2 $:

$ \Delta E = -3.40 - (-13.6) = 10.2\ \text{eV} $

$ \lambda = \frac{1240}{10.2} = 121.6\ \text{nm} $

**Both lie deep in the ultraviolet**, which is why the Lyman series is invisible to the eye and was discovered only with photographic and vacuum-spectrograph techniques.

**Why every series converges.** The energy levels crowd towards $ E = 0 $, so the transitions bunch up towards the series limit — the lines get closer and closer together and then stop. Beyond the limit lies a *continuum*, corresponding to a free electron with kinetic energy to spare.

**Contrast the Balmer series** (ending at $ n = 2 $), whose limit is $ 365 $ nm and whose longest line is the $ 656 $ nm H-alpha — putting four of its lines in the visible band.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Excitation by electron collision
worked_examples.problem: Electrons of kinetic energy $ 12.5 $ eV bombard ground-state hydrogen atoms. Which levels can be excited, and what wavelengths will be emitted?
worked_examples.solution:
**Energy needed for each excitation** from $ n = 1 $ at $ -13.6 $ eV:

To $ n = 2 $ ($ -3.40 $ eV): $ 10.2 $ eV ✓ available

To $ n = 3 $ ($ -1.51 $ eV): $ 12.1 $ eV ✓ available

To $ n = 4 $ ($ -0.85 $ eV): $ 12.75 $ eV ✗ exceeds $ 12.5 $ eV

**So excitation reaches $ n = 3 $ at most.**

**Emitted wavelengths.** Three transitions are possible:

$ 3 \to 2 $: $ 1.89 $ eV → $ 656 $ nm

$ 3 \to 1 $: $ 12.1 $ eV → $ 102 $ nm

$ 2 \to 1 $: $ 10.2 $ eV → $ 122 $ nm

**Why the electron may give up only part of its energy.** A colliding electron is free to transfer any amount, keeping the rest as kinetic energy — so $ 12.5 $ eV electrons can excite the $ 10.2 $ eV or $ 12.1 $ eV transitions and carry on with the remainder.

**Contrast with photon absorption.** A photon must be absorbed whole, so only photons of *exactly* $ 10.2 $, $ 12.1 $ eV and so on can excite the atom. This difference between collisional and radiative excitation is exactly what the Franck-Hertz experiment demonstrated.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — Speed and period of the electron
worked_examples.problem: Find the electron's speed in the ground state of hydrogen, and the number of revolutions it makes per second.
worked_examples.solution:
**Speed from the quantisation condition.** With $ mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi} $ and $ r_1 = 53 $ pm:

$ v = \frac{h}{2\pi m r} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2\pi(9.1 \times 10^{-31})(53 \times 10^{-12})} $

$ = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{3.03 \times 10^{-40}} = 2.19 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Revolutions per second:**

$ f = \frac{v}{2\pi r} = \frac{2.19 \times 10^{6}}{2\pi(53 \times 10^{-12})} = \frac{2.19 \times 10^{6}}{3.33 \times 10^{-10}} = 6.6 \times 10^{15}\ \text{s}^{-1} $

**Six and a half thousand million million orbits per second.** This is why an atom appears to have a smooth, static electron cloud on any observable timescale.

**Note the fine-structure constant hiding here.** $ v/c = 2.19 \times 10^{6}/3 \times 10^{8} = 1/137 $ — the electron in hydrogen moves at $ 0.73\% $ of light speed. That the ratio is small is why non-relativistic Bohr theory works as well as it does; that it is not *zero* is why fine structure exists at all.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Number of spectral lines from an excited level
worked_examples.problem: A hydrogen sample is excited to the $ n = 5 $ level. How many distinct spectral lines can it emit, and how many of them belong to the Balmer series?
worked_examples.solution:
**Total number of lines.** Every pair of levels from 1 to 5 gives one transition:

$ N = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10 $

**Balmer lines** — those ending at $ n = 2 $:

$ 5 \to 2 $, $ 4 \to 2 $, $ 3 \to 2 $ — **three** lines.

**The full breakdown.**

Lyman (to $ n=1 $): $ 5\to1, 4\to1, 3\to1, 2\to1 $ — 4 lines

Balmer (to $ n=2 $): 3 lines

Paschen (to $ n=3 $): $ 5\to3, 4\to3 $ — 2 lines

Brackett (to $ n=4 $): $ 5\to4 $ — 1 line

Total $ 4+3+2+1 = 10 $ ✓

**Why the counting formula works.** Choosing any 2 of the $ n $ levels defines one transition, and $ \binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} $. Note that a *single* atom emits only one cascade of at most $ n-1 $ photons; seeing all ten lines requires a sample of many atoms taking different routes down.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Rydberg constant from the Bohr model
worked_examples.problem: Use the Bohr energy levels to find the Rydberg constant, and check it against the H-alpha wavelength.
worked_examples.solution:
**The Bohr result** written in wavenumber form:

$ \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{\Delta E}{hc} = \frac{13.6}{hc}\left(\frac{1}{n_1^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right) $

So $ R = \frac{13.6\ \text{eV}}{hc} $.

**Evaluate**, with $ 13.6\ \text{eV} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} $ J:

$ R = \frac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})} = \frac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{1.989 \times 10^{-25}} $

$ = 1.096 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1} $

The accepted value is $ 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1} $ ✓

**Check against H-alpha ($ 3 \to 2 $):**

$ \frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = (1.097 \times 10^{7})(0.1389) = 1.524 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1} $

$ \lambda = 656\ \text{nm} $ ✓ — matching the earlier calculation.

**Why this was Bohr's decisive triumph.** The Rydberg constant had been *measured* spectroscopically for decades with no explanation. Bohr's model derived it from $ m $, $ e $, $ h $ and $ \varepsilon_0 $ alone — an entirely independent route to a known number, agreeing to four figures.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — Recoil and the limits of the model
worked_examples.problem: Explain why the Bohr model gives slightly different spectral wavelengths for hydrogen and deuterium, even though both have $ Z = 1 $.
worked_examples.solution:
**The flaw in treating the nucleus as fixed.** Both the electron and the nucleus orbit their common centre of mass. The correct treatment replaces the electron mass $ m $ by the *reduced mass*

$ \mu = \frac{m M}{m + M} $

where $ M $ is the nuclear mass.

**For hydrogen** ($ M \approx 1836m $):

$ \mu = \frac{1836}{1837}m = 0.99946m $

**For deuterium** ($ M \approx 3672m $):

$ \mu = \frac{3672}{3673}m = 0.99973m $

**Effect on the spectrum.** Since $ E \propto \mu $, deuterium's levels are deeper by a factor of about $ 1.00027 $, so its lines sit at slightly *shorter* wavelengths. For H-alpha at $ 656.3 $ nm the shift is about $ 0.18 $ nm — small, but easily resolved.

**How this was used.** Urey discovered deuterium in 1932 by spotting exactly these faint companion lines beside the hydrogen ones, and won the Nobel Prize for it. A refinement to a model can be as informative as the model itself.
